newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Protests grow over Taipei-Pyongyang nuclear deal.
newsitem.headline: Protests grow over Taipei-Pyongyang nuclear deal.

text.p: Protesters held demonstrations in Seoul and a South Korean anti-nuclear delegation arrived in Taipei as the dispute over Taiwan's plans to ship nuclear waste to North Korea intensified.

The 12-member anti-nuclear delegation, which included four South Korean congressmen, arrived in Taipei on Friday to pressure Taipei to cancel the deal with Pyongyang to ship up to 200,000 barrels of nuclear waste to the impoverished communist state.

Members of the group told reporters on their arrival that they wanted to meet Taiwan officials and environmentalists to discuss their concern over the agreement, signed on January 11 by the state-run Taiwan Power Company and a North Korean agency.

Their visit came just a day after Taiwan deported seven South Korean activists for breaching local assembly laws by holding a protest in Taipei. The activists had also clashed with a group of local residents who supported the plan.
In Seoul, 10 South Korean environmental activists began what they called an indefinite hunger strike outside Taiwan's trade office, witnesses said.
The activists, including seven members of Green Korea expelled from Taiwan on Thursday, were stopped by police from pitching tents.
Nearby, in central Seoul, hundreds of riot police scuffled with more than 100 demonstrators wearing red headbands over masks depicting skulls.
The demonstrators, members of a Christian youth group, shouted slogans calling for the cancellation of the nuclear-waste deal.
Taiwan's government on Friday reiterated its determination to press ahead with the waste shipments, despite the growing pressure from South Korea and China -- Taiwan's arch rival.
The four South Korean legislators, accompanied by several environmental professors and researchers, are due to meet officials of the Taipei government and Taiwan Power Co.
China on Thursday criticised the deal, saying it was a blatant attempt by Taipei to spoil Beijing's ties with its communist neighbour.
China has considered Taiwan a renegade province since a civil war split them in 1949.
Taiwan has no diplomatic ties with North or South Korea, both of which recognise Beijing.
South Korea, worried about possible nuclear contamination on the Korean peninsula, says there is no proof the North -- Seoul's arch-rival -- can store the waste safely.
Last Saturday, scores of South Koreans burned the Taiwanese national flag and President Lee Tung-hui in effigy, provoking outrage in Taiwan.
Taiwan maintains the Taipei-Pyongyang waste pact complies with all international regulations and that shipments would be securely contained in steel barrels.
The U.S. State Department said on Wednesday that any shipment of nuclear waste from Taiwan to North Korea should conform to international standards.
